messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Interesting plot shape - theta vs. SE - EAP estimation
parts:
Thanks, it's what I expected. Because the test is so long (500+ items) the precision of the thetas can be really small, so the course integration gride used to compute EAP estimates will miss the more minute differences between the associated estimates (basically, the numerical integration is too course given how tight each posterior function is, so you get this back-and-forth between the quadrature nodes). Model estimates don't suffer from this problem as they are based on the highest point + quadratic behaviour of the posterior only, and in this case I would certainly prefer them to EAPs.

In any event, to fix this in very long tests like this just increase the quadpts argument, like the following:

mirt_thetas0 <- as.data.frame(fscores(mirt_model, full.scores.SE = TRUE)) # original with 61 quadrature
mirt_thetas1 <- as.data.frame(fscores(mirt_model, full.scores.SE = TRUE, quadpts = 401)) # many more 

layout(matrix(1:2, 1))
plot(mirt_thetas0)
plot(mirt_thetas1)



Also, you might want to consider increasing the quadrature number when estimating this model as well since it might improve the IRT estimate precision as well, leading to an even more precise model. HTH.

Phil

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Interesting plot shape - theta vs. SE - EAP estimation
parts:
That was a typo (I meant modal estimates, as in the highest point of some density function). And to answer your question about numerical integration it's really just a trial and error approach until the error is sufficiently small, or the solution stops improving.  E.g., if you increase the default quadrature from 61 to 101 and saw no difference in the final observed log-likelihood, there's not much being gained from the added numerical precision. Adaptive quadrature rules of course exist, which aim to minimize the integration error explicitly, but they are generally quite heavy computationally in the context of estimating IRT models for tests with a moderate number of items. HTH.

Phil
